figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Motivation and overview of Meta2. Offline evolution produces a shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot adapt to evidence revealed during a new run, while online methods face limitations in intervention timing, knowledge guidance, and verifier availability. By moving offline optimization one level up, Meta2 learns a reusable Meta-Skill from contrastive training rollouts and freezes it to guide task-local harness evolution at checkpoints online, without access to verifier feedback at test-time. Across both evaluated benchmarks, this design yields the highest performance among the compared methods.
figures.headline: Meta2 reaches the highest performance among compared methods on both benchmarks, using a frozen Meta-Skill and no test-time verifier feedback.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Design of Meta2: offline knowledge learning, online harness evolution and format of Meta-Skill. Offline, rollouts are collected under three conditions: the task agent alone (A), evolution guided by the current Meta-Skill (B), and evolution with verifier knowledge (C). Deterministic pairing of terminal outcomes yields act, avoid, and hold contrasts. LLM-based reflection and cross-task aggregation distill these contrasts into reusable lessons, which iteratively update the Meta-Skill. Online, the frozen Meta-Skill guides an evolver LLM to retain or modify the harness at deterministic checkpoints, while the task agent continues along a single trajectory in one environment. Meta-Skill entries specify when, how and why to intervene with reference examples.
figures.headline: Three-condition rollouts produce contrasts that refine a Meta-Skill, which guides KEEP or EVOLVE decisions at checkpoints during online runs.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 2, Meta2 has three main components: a checkpoint-based interface for within-run evolution, an offline procedure that learns $\mathcal{M}$, and a deployment protocol that reuses $\mathcal{M}$ without held-out verifier feedback.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Checkpoint-interval sensitivity. Performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus log-scaled online cost.
figures.headline: Terminal-Bench 2.1 performance peaks at checkpoint interval 5 with 81.00%, while more frequent checkpoints raise cost without gains.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Component ablations. The first four settings evaluate the online evolver and two Meta-Skill construction methods. The fifth retains online edits across tasks instead of resetting to $h^{(0)}$.
figures.headline: Adding the online evolver lifts both benchmarks, contrastive Meta-Skill reaches 81.00 and 44.44, and keeping edits across tasks lowers both.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Early intervention guided by an act entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). The task requires a Git push to deploy hello.html to a web server on port 8080. At the first checkpoint, the evolver without Meta-Skill specifies an implementation and requests validation only “where feasible.” The task agent tests in a temporary sandbox but does not run the installer in the task environment; the evolver accepts the result despite the missing /git/server directory and inactive service. With Meta-Skill, entry E-02 guides the evolver to require end-to-end evidence: a clone, commit, and push followed by a fresh HTTP request confirming that the deployed page returns “hello world.” The task agent installs the service and verifies this sequence, after which the evolver chooses KEEP at the subsequent and terminal checkpoints.
figures.headline: An act entry makes the evolver require end-to-end deployment evidence, after which the task agent installs the service and verifies the page.
citing_sentences: Figures 6–8 illustrate the three Meta-Skill entry types: act, where guidance supports an early or mid-run intervention; avoid, where guidance discourages a particular intervention; and hold, where guidance supports leaving the harness unchanged.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Avoiding premature redirection with an avoid entry (Terminal-Bench 2.1). By checkpoint $t_{3}$, both task agents have identified the bundled Rave warrior as a promising candidate, but its performance against stone remains below the required threshold. Without Meta-Skill, the evolver uses its final notice to redirect exploration toward other bundled warriors. The task agent constructs an Aeka–Rave hybrid but finishes with 74 wins against stone, one short of the required 75. With Meta-Skill, entry E-06 discourages changing the search strategy while exploration continues to make progress. The evolver chooses KEEP at $t_{3}$ and subsequent checkpoints, allowing the task agent to continue tuning Rave and satisfy all five performance thresholds.
figures.headline: An avoid entry stops the evolver from redirecting a still-improving search, letting the task agent keep tuning and meet all five thresholds.
citing_sentences: Figures 6–8 illustrate the three Meta-Skill entry types: act, where guidance supports an early or mid-run intervention; avoid, where guidance discourages a particular intervention; and hold, where guidance supports leaving the harness unchanged.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Performance versus full cost with GPT-5.6-Terra. Full cost includes one-time offline construction and online evaluation costs, plotted on a logarithmic horizontal scale. Dashed lines connect the non-dominated performance–cost point estimates for Terminal-Bench 2.1 (left) and DeepSWE 1.1 (right).
figures.headline: Meta2 lies on the cost-performance Pareto frontier on both benchmarks with GPT-5.6-Terra, including one-time offline construction cost.
citing_sentences: With the highest observed performance among evaluated methods, Meta2 lies on the performance–cost Pareto frontier on both benchmarks, as shown in Figure 9 in Appendix E.2.
Figure 9 compares held-out performance against full cost for GPT-5.6-Terra on both benchmarks.

abstract: Harness optimization improves long-horizon agents by refining the prompts, tools, memory, and hooks around a frozen model. Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness that may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during, or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch or rely on verifier feedback that is usually unavailable at test time. We introduce Meta$^2$, which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta$^2$ learns a textual Meta-Skill $M$ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of $M$, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine $M$ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen $M$ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit applies to the rest of the same run without resetting its environment or progress. Thus, evolution guidance transfers across tasks while harness edits remain task-local, and held-out verifier feedback is never available to the evolver. On two long-horizon benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1, Meta$^2$ achieves the highest performance among evaluated methods with GPT-5.6-Terra, reaching 81.00% and 44.44%, respectively. Ablations support the value of contrastive evolution guidance and keeping online harness edits task-local.

sections.body: The section argues that a harness fixed before execution must anticipate situations that appear only during a run. Offline optimization yields one shared harness that may overfit training tasks. Online evolvers can edit within a run, but they must decide when to intervene without verifier feedback. Meta2 precomputes a textual Meta-Skill offline from training rollouts under three conditions: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current Meta-Skill, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only in training. At deployment the Meta-Skill is frozen, and each edit applies only to the rest of its run. The section reports 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra. It notes that the contrasts give directional evidence and do not establish the causal effect of any single checkpoint decision.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Shared offline harnesses cannot react to evidence revealed during a run, so Meta2 learns reusable guidance for task-local online edits.

sections.body:
This section defines a task instance as an instruction, an environment, and a verifier whose criteria the agent and evolver cannot observe. A task agent combines a model with a harness of prompts, context policy, tools, skills, memory, and hooks. Harness evolution is formalized as an evolver that proposes an edit at each decision from the current harness and the available evidence:

$$
\delta^{(k)}\sim g(\cdot\mid h^{(k-1)},\mathcal{I}^{(k)})
$$

Offline evolution uses training trajectories and outcomes to output one shared harness. Online evolution is split into pre-run, within-run, and after-run settings by when an edit is selected and which executions it affects. The section argues that only within-run evolution can respond to an unfinished attempt, but its decisions cannot depend on that attempt's eventual verifier outcome.
sections.heading: Background: Harness Evolution
sections.headline: Harness evolution is framed by when edits are chosen and what evidence they use: offline, pre-run, within-run, or after-run.

sections.body: Meta2 keeps the model and seed harness fixed and optimizes only the evolver's Meta-Skill. Online, a checkpoint interface gives the evolver the new trajectory delta, read-only workspace observations, and the status of the preceding edit. The evolver then chooses KEEP or EVOLVE. Offline, each training task is run under three conditions. Five contrast directions follow: B-pass/A-fail and C-pass/B-fail give act evidence, B-fail/A-pass and C-fail/B-pass give avoid evidence, and A-pass/B-pass gives hold evidence. REFLECT, AGGREGATE, and UPDATE turn these contrasts into entries. AGGREGATE keeps only guidance supported by at least two distinct tasks. Each deployed run restarts from the seed harness, and online decisions are never written back to the Meta-Skill.
sections.heading: Meta2: Precomputing Reusable Knowledge for Online Evolution
sections.headline: Meta2 freezes a Meta-Skill learned from three-condition rollout contrasts and uses it at checkpoints to choose KEEP or EVOLVE per run.

sections.body: The section compares Meta2 with human-designed, self-evolution, and harness-evolution baselines on Terminal-Bench 2.1, scored as mean@5, and DeepSWE 1.1, scored as mean@3. With GPT-5.6-Terra, Meta2 reaches 81.00% and 44.44%, which the section reports as gains of 14.67 and 9.77 points over the NexAU seed harness. The strongest harness-evolution baseline, Meta-Harness, gains 7.00 and 2.66 points. Several self-evolution methods fall below the seed on DeepSWE. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 on Terminal-Bench, Meta2 reaches 77.67%. A separate Meta-Skill is built for each backbone, so this tests robustness across backbones rather than transfer of a frozen Meta-Skill. Offline and online costs are reported separately in US dollars, and the comparisons use point estimates.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On two benchmarks with GPT-5.6-Terra, Meta2 scores highest, at 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1.

sections.body: This section groups prior work by when edits are selected. Offline methods optimize prompts, pipelines, or harness code on training tasks and deploy one fixed artifact. Pre-run and after-run methods adapt either before execution or only for later attempts. Within-run methods such as Continual Harness, PILOT, and Live-SWE-agent adapt during a run, but without learned guidance on when to intervene. The section positions Meta2 as a hybrid. It learns reusable evolution knowledge offline in the form of a Meta-Skill that records when to act, hold, or avoid an intervention. It then applies that knowledge to task-local edits within each run, without held-out verifier feedback. Table 6 and Table 7 in Appendix G summarize these distinctions.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior harness methods either fix one harness offline or adapt online without guidance, while Meta2 combines offline knowledge with task-local edits.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the method. Meta2 learns reusable evolution knowledge offline, freezes it, and uses it with active-run evidence so that harness edits stay local to each run. It repeats the reported results: 81.00% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 44.44% on DeepSWE 1.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra, and 77.67% on Terminal-Bench with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. It states that ablations support contrastive Meta-Skill learning and resetting the harness between tasks. The closing principle is to precompute how to adapt, then adapt locally as the task unfolds.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Precompute how to adapt, then adapt locally, with ablations supporting contrastive learning and per-task resets.

sections.body: The appendix contains the notation table, the offline Meta-Skill construction and online checkpoint procedures, and dataset details. Terminal-Bench 2.1 has 29 training and 60 test tasks, and DeepSWE 1.1 has 38 training and 75 test tasks. It also gives baseline settings, implementation details, mean and standard deviation across repeated runs, and a cost-performance Pareto analysis. Further sections give the evolver and offline-stage prompts, the Meta-Skill entry fields in Table 8, and the content of the Meta-Skill entries. Case studies of act, avoid, and hold entries are included, along with a limitations section.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists notation, algorithm details, dataset splits and baselines, prompts, Meta-Skill entry format, and case studies.
